reasons: Immutability is claimed but not enforced in this file.
No tests or enforcement code are shown.

terms.meaning: a permanent log of actions taken in the app
role-based access control, rules that depend on a user's role
a link from one table to a row in another table
a flexible text format for nested data

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and setup
sections.what: Brings in the column types, the link to the shared base and the portable UUID type.
sections.why: Likely reason: the three table classes below need these tools.
sections.watch_out: The UUID alias is chosen so the same code runs on PostgreSQL and SQLite. Changing it affects every table.

sections.name: AuditLog
sections.title: Audit trail table
sections.what: Defines a table that records each action with what happened, who did it, what it touched, from where, and when.
sections.why: Likely reason: a permanent trail for review and accountability.
sections.watch_out: Nothing here stops rows from being edited or deleted, so the immutable promise depends on other code.

sections.name: FieldPermission
sections.title: Field permission rules
sections.what: Defines a table saying whether a given role may read or write a given field on a given table.
sections.why: Likely reason: controls who sees or changes each field without writing code for each one.
sections.watch_out: Both flags default to off, so a missing flag means no access, but the code that reads them is not shown.

sections.name: SystemConfig
sections.title: System settings table
sections.what: Defines a table of named settings, each with a unique key, a JSON value, and who changed it last and when.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps app-wide settings in the database so they can change without a code edit.
sections.watch_out: The key must be unique, so saving a second value for the same key fails unless the code updates the existing row.

summary: Defines three tables for the audit trail, field-level permissions, and system settings.
purpose: Stores who did what and when, which role may read or write each field, and named system settings.
why: Likely reason: a traceable record of actions is needed for review. The docstring calls the audit log immutable.
how: 1) Each class maps to one table. 2) Audit rows record the action, the acting user, the target, the request address and the browser. 3) Field permission rows hold one row per role, table and field, with read and write flags. 4) System config rows hold one JSON value per unique key.
inputs: Written by app code that performs actions, plus the user and request details.
outputs: Rows in the audit_logs, field_permissions and system_config tables.
risks: The audit log is described as immutable, but nothing in this file stops edits or deletes. Permissions are stored here, but enforcement code is not shown. Config values are free-form, so a bad value is not caught here.
debug: If audit entries are missing, check the code that calls the audit writer. If permissions seem ignored, check whether any code reads field_permissions.
